blocks.content: GANDHIAN MASS STRUGGLE – COMPLETE & EXHAUSTIVE EXPLANATION

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The period between 1919 and 1934 marks the core phase of the Gandhian mass struggle in the Indian freedom movement.
The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre in 1919 served as major catalysts for nationwide trauma and political awakening.
The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922) served as India's first nationwide mass movement alongside the Khilafat Movement for Hindu-Muslim unity.
The Swarajist Phase (1923–1927) focused on political resistance through legislative council entry.
The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1934) directly defied colonial laws, leading to the Round Table Conferences and Poona Pact of 1932.

blocks.content: 1. Introduction: Why 1919–1934 is the CORE of Indian Freedom Struggle

The period from 1919 to 1934 is regarded as the most decisive phase of the Indian National Movement because it transformed the freedom struggle from an elite-led political movement into a truly mass-based revolution. Under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, millions of Indians—peasants, workers, women, students, tribals, and even sections of the urban poor—actively participated in nationalist activities. This era institutionalised Gandhian techniques of Satyagraha, Ahimsa, non-cooperation, civil disobedience, and constructive work. Politically, this phase shattered the moral legitimacy of British rule and made independence an irreversible national demand.
2. Background: Impact of World War I on India

India’s participation in the First World War placed enormous economic and social burdens on the country. The British extracted men, money, and material from India, promising constitutional reforms in return. However, instead of meaningful self-government, India was rewarded with repression.

• Sharp rise in prices and inflation

• Heavy taxation and war loans

• Shortage of essential commodities

• Decline in real wages of workers

• Increased rural indebtedness
Indian leaders who had supported the British war effort felt betrayed. The gap between British promises and actual policies widened nationalist anger.
3. Rowlatt Act (1919): Black Law Explained in Depth

The Rowlatt Act was based on the recommendations of the Rowlatt Committee. It authorised the British government to imprison Indians without trial, suspend habeas corpus, and curb civil liberties. Indians unanimously opposed this Act, calling it a ‘Black Act’.
Gandhi called for nationwide hartals, fasting, and peaceful protests. This marked his first all-India political movement.
4. Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (1919): National Trauma

On 13 April 1919, a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar was brutally fired upon by General Dyer without warning. Hundreds of unarmed men, women, and children were killed. This event deeply shocked the Indian conscience and destroyed any remaining faith in British justice and moral authority.

• Nationwide outrage

• Radicalisation of Indian politics

• Emergence of mass nationalism

• Tagore renounced his knighthood
5. Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–1922): First Nationwide Mass Movement
The Non-Cooperation Movement represented the first major attempt to challenge British authority through organised, non-violent mass resistance.

• Jallianwala Bagh Massacre

• Rowlatt Act repression

• Khilafat issue

• Failure of Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms

• Boycott of government schools, colleges, and courts

• Boycott of foreign goods

• Surrender of titles

• Promotion of khadi and charkha

• Peaceful picketing of liquor shops
The movement spread to towns and villages alike. Students left schools, lawyers gave up practice, peasants organised protests, and women entered public life in large numbers.
Violence at Chauri Chaura, where protesters burnt a police station, prompted Gandhi to withdraw the movement, reaffirming his commitment to non-violence.
6. Khilafat Movement: Hindu–Muslim Unity Explained
The Khilafat Movement aimed to protect the position of the Turkish Caliph after World War I. Gandhi supported the movement to build Hindu–Muslim unity and broaden the base of nationalism.
7. Swarajist Phase (1923–1927): Council Entry Explained
After the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation, a debate arose within Congress. C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party to enter legislative councils and obstruct British governance from within.
8. Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1934): Defying Colonial Laws
The Civil Disobedience Movement marked a new stage in Gandhian struggle by openly violating unjust colonial laws.
Salt was chosen because it affected every Indian. Gandhi’s Dandi March symbolised moral defiance and united the nation.
People manufactured salt, refused taxes, and boycotted British goods. The movement saw massive participation but also severe repression.
9. Round Table Conferences (1930–1932): Constitutional Deadlock
The British convened Round Table Conferences to discuss constitutional reforms, but their exclusionary nature and communal divisions led to failure.
This pact temporarily suspended Civil Disobedience and allowed Gandhi to attend the Second Round Table Conference.
10. Communal Award & Poona Pact (1932)

items: Chronology Trap: Memorize the exact order of movements—Rowlatt Act (1919) -> Non-Cooperation (1920–1922) -> Swarajist Phase (1923–1927) -> Civil Disobedience (1930–1934).
Pay special attention to 1932 constitutional developments, specifically the Communal Award and the Poona Pact.
Distinguish between the council entry strategy of the Swarajists (1923–1927) and direct law defiance during the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1934).

blocks.content: The Communal Award granted separate electorates to Depressed Classes. Gandhi opposed it, leading to the Poona Pact with B.R. Ambedkar, which provided reserved seats instead.
11. Withdrawal of Civil Disobedience (1934)
Continuous repression, economic hardship, and limited success led Gandhi to suspend the movement in 1934.
12. Overall Significance of 1919–1934 Phase
This phase permanently transformed Indian politics. Gandhi became the undisputed leader, mass nationalism became irreversible, and the struggle entered its final decisive stage.
